castles-of-the-middle-rhine.title: Castles of the Middle Rhine
castles-of-the-middle-rhine.lead: From the fortress above Koblenz upstream to Bingen, along the gorge where a castle stands on almost every bend.
castles-of-the-middle-rhine.intro: Between Koblenz and Bingen the Rhine cuts a narrow gorge through slate hills, and for some sixty-five kilometres castles follow one another on both banks. The valley is a World Heritage Site. The route starts at Stolzenfels, just above Koblenz, crosses to the fortress of Ehrenbreitstein and goes up the right bank, past Marksburg, the only hilltop castle here that was never destroyed, and the toll castle on its island at Kaub, then crosses by ferry for the three castles above Trechtingshausen. There are no bridges on this stretch, so the ferries are part of the trip.

bavaria-from-wurzburg-to-neuschwanstein.title: Bavaria: from Würzburg to Neuschwanstein
bavaria-from-wurzburg-to-neuschwanstein.lead: South along the Romantic Road, from a bishop's palace on the Main to the castles of Ludwig II at the foot of the Alps.
bavaria-from-wurzburg-to-neuschwanstein.intro: The route follows the line of the Romantic Road through Franconia and Swabia into Upper Bavaria. It starts in Würzburg, with the Residence and the fortress across the river, passes the walled town of Nördlingen and Harburg Castle above the Wörnitz, and reaches Augsburg. From there the land rises towards the Alps: the pilgrimage church of Wies in its meadow, then Neuschwanstein, and over the hills Linderhof, the smallest of the king's palaces and the only one he saw finished.

tuscany-florence-to-the-val-d-orcia.title: Tuscany: Florence to the Val d'Orcia
tuscany-florence-to-the-val-d-orcia.lead: Florence, Lucca, Pisa, San Gimignano and Siena, then south into the hills of the Val d'Orcia.
tuscany-florence-to-the-val-d-orcia.intro: A loop through the cities that made Tuscany what it is, ending in its best-known landscape. Florence comes first, with the cathedral, the Uffizi and the old bridge within a few minutes' walk of each other. The route then heads west to Lucca, inside its walls, and to Pisa, turns back inland for the towers of San Gimignano and the shell-shaped square of Siena, and finishes among the cypress-lined roads between Pienza and the Val d'Orcia.
stops: Collegiata di Santa Maria Assunta, San Gimignano

sicily-temples-and-cathedrals.title: Sicily: temples and cathedrals
sicily-temples-and-cathedrals.lead: Around the island from Cefalù to Taormina: Norman cathedrals in the north, Greek temples in the south, baroque towns in the east.
sicily-temples-and-cathedrals.intro: Sicily was Greek, Roman, Arab and Norman before it was Italian, and this route passes through all of it. It begins with the Norman cathedrals of Cefalù, Palermo and Monreale, with their gold mosaics, then follows the west and south coasts past the Greek temples of Segesta, Selinunte and Agrigento. Inland, the Roman villa near Piazza Armerina keeps one of the largest sets of floor mosaics anywhere. The last days belong to the east: baroque Noto, Syracuse with its cathedral built into a Greek temple, and the theatre of Taormina facing Etna.

chateaux-of-the-loire-valley.title: Châteaux of the Loire Valley
chateaux-of-the-loire-valley.lead: Chambord, Blois, Cheverny, Amboise, Chenonceau, Villandry and Azay-le-Rideau: the houses the French court built along its river.
chateaux-of-the-loire-valley.intro: For a century and a half the kings of France lived on the Loire, and the court built where the king was. The result is the densest group of Renaissance houses in Europe, most of them within an hour of Tours. The route comes down the river from Chambord, the largest, with its double staircase, to Blois and Cheverny, then to Amboise, where Leonardo da Vinci spent his last years at the Clos Lucé. Chenonceau spans the Cher on its arches. West of Tours come the gardens of Villandry, Azay-le-Rideau on its island and Ussé at the edge of the forest of Chinon.

roman-provence.title: Roman Provence
roman-provence.lead: Orange, Avignon, the Pont du Gard, Nîmes and Arles: two thousand years of stone within an hour's drive of each other.
roman-provence.intro: The lower Rhône valley has the densest group of Roman monuments in France, most of them still standing to their full height. The route starts at the theatre of Orange, whose stage wall is intact, stops in Avignon for the palace of the popes and the broken bridge, then crosses to the three-tiered aqueduct over the Gardon. It ends with the temple of Nîmes, among the best preserved of the Roman world, and the amphitheatre of Arles, still in use.

andalusia-seville-to-cordoba.title: Andalusia: Seville to Córdoba
andalusia-seville-to-cordoba.lead: Seville, Jerez, Cádiz, Ronda, Málaga, Granada and Córdoba, through the south that the Moors and the Castilians both built.
andalusia-seville-to-cordoba.intro: For nearly eight centuries the south of Spain was Al-Andalus, and its great buildings are either Moorish or built on top of something Moorish. The route starts in Seville, where the cathedral stands on the site of the mosque and keeps its minaret as a bell tower, and the royal palace is still in use. It goes down to Jerez and to Cádiz on its peninsula, climbs to Ronda, reaches the coast at Málaga and turns inland to Granada, for the Alhambra and the gardens of the Generalife. It ends in Córdoba, in the forest of columns of the Mosque-Cathedral.
stops: Alcázar of Jerez de la Frontera

castles-and-fortified-churches-of-transy.title: Castles and fortified churches of Transylvania
castles-and-fortified-churches-of-transy.lead: From Peleș over the mountains to Bran and Brașov, through the Saxon villages to Sighișoara and Sibiu, and on to Corvin Castle.
castles-and-fortified-churches-of-transy.intro: The route crosses the Carpathians at Sinaia, where the Romanian kings built Peleș, and comes down into Transylvania past the peasant citadel of Râșnov and Bran Castle. Beyond Brașov and its Black Church lie the villages founded by Saxon settlers in the twelfth century, who fortified their churches instead of building castles: Prejmer, Viscri and Biertan are the best known. Sighișoara is a walled town that is still lived in, Sibiu was the Saxon capital, and Alba Iulia keeps a star-shaped fortress from the eighteenth century. The last stop is Corvin Castle in Hunedoara, the largest Gothic castle in the country.

painted-monasteries-of-bucovina.title: Painted monasteries of Bucovina
painted-monasteries-of-bucovina.lead: Voroneț, Humor, Moldovița, Sucevița and their neighbours in northern Moldavia, in the order the road links them.
painted-monasteries-of-bucovina.intro: In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries the princes of Moldavia built a group of monasteries in the hills around Suceava and had several of them painted on the outside as well as inside. The frescoes have survived five hundred winters, and eight of the churches are World Heritage Sites. The route starts at the fortress of Suceava, goes north to Dragomirna, Arbore and Putna, crosses the hills to Sucevița and Moldovița, and comes back down through Humor to Voroneț, known for the blue of its Last Judgement. The distances are short, but the roads are slow.

castles-of-scotland.title: Castles of Scotland
castles-of-scotland.lead: Edinburgh and Stirling, up the east coast to Dunnottar, across the Highlands to Loch Ness and Eilean Donan, and back by Inveraray.
castles-of-scotland.intro: A circuit of the mainland that takes in the two royal castles, a cliff-top ruin, a castle on Loch Ness and one on a tidal island. Edinburgh and Stirling both stand on volcanic rock and controlled the way north. Glamis is a lived-in house with towers, Dunnottar a ruin above the North Sea. From there the route crosses to Urquhart Castle on Loch Ness, continues west to Eilean Donan, where three sea lochs meet, and returns south by Inveraray on Loch Fyne. The roads in the west are narrow; allow more time than the distances suggest.

castles-of-north-wales.title: Castles of North Wales
castles-of-north-wales.lead: Conwy, Beaumaris, Caernarfon and Harlech: the four fortresses Edward I built to hold Wales.
castles-of-north-wales.intro: After conquering Gwynedd in the 1280s, Edward I of England had a ring of castles built along the coast, most of them by the same master mason, James of St George. Four of them are together a World Heritage Site, and they are among the most complete medieval fortresses in Europe. Conwy and Caernarfon still have their town walls. Beaumaris, on Anglesey, was never finished but has the most regular plan of all, and Harlech stands on a rock above the dunes, looking across to Snowdonia.

bohemia-prague-to-cesky-krumlov.title: Bohemia: Prague to Český Krumlov
bohemia-prague-to-cesky-krumlov.lead: Prague, the castles of Karlštejn and Konopiště, the silver town of Kutná Hora, Telč and Český Krumlov.
bohemia-prague-to-cesky-krumlov.intro: The route begins in Prague, at the castle above the river and the bridge below it, and then makes a wide loop through Bohemia and the edge of Moravia. Karlštejn was built by Charles IV to keep the crown jewels; Konopiště was the last home of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Kutná Hora grew rich on silver and built a cathedral to show it, and has a chapel decorated with human bones. Telč has one of the most complete Renaissance squares in Europe. The route ends in Český Krumlov, where a castle second in size only to Prague's rises above a bend of the Vltava.

classical-greece.title: Classical Greece
classical-greece.lead: Athens, Corinth, Mycenae, Epidaurus, Olympia and Delphi, with the rock monasteries of Meteora at the end.
classical-greece.intro: The classic circuit of the Greek mainland. It starts on the Acropolis of Athens, crosses the isthmus to the fortress above Corinth, and goes round the Peloponnese: Mycenae with its Lion Gate, the theatre of Epidaurus, where a whisper on stage reaches the top row, and Olympia, where the games were held for more than a thousand years. The route then crosses the gulf to Delphi on the slope of Mount Parnassus, and continues north to Meteora, where monasteries were built on top of sandstone pillars.

portugal-lisbon-to-tomar.title: Portugal: Lisbon to Tomar
portugal-lisbon-to-tomar.lead: The monastery of Belém, the palaces of Sintra, walled Óbidos, and the monasteries of Batalha and Tomar.
portugal-lisbon-to-tomar.intro: A short route north of Lisbon through the buildings Portugal put up when it was richest. The Jerónimos Monastery in Belém was paid for by the spice trade and is the best example of the Manueline style, with its carved ropes and sea motifs. Sintra, in the hills, has the old royal palace with its two conical chimneys and the coloured Pena Palace above it. Óbidos is a small town entirely inside its walls. Batalha was built to give thanks for a victory over Castile, and the Convent of Christ in Tomar was the seat of the Knights Templar in Portugal.

croatia-from-istria-to-dubrovnik.title: Croatia: from Istria to Dubrovnik
croatia-from-istria-to-dubrovnik.lead: Down the Adriatic from Poreč and Pula to Split and Dubrovnik, with the lakes of Plitvice and the falls of Krka on the way.
croatia-from-istria-to-dubrovnik.intro: The length of the Croatian coast, with two detours inland. Istria comes first: the sixth-century mosaics of the basilica in Poreč and the Roman arena of Pula, one of the largest still standing. The route then leaves the sea for the Plitvice Lakes, a chain of sixteen lakes joined by waterfalls, and returns to it at the Krka river. Trogir is a medieval town on an island, Split grew inside the palace of a Roman emperor, and Dubrovnik, at the end of the road, can be walked all the way round on top of its walls.

krakow-and-southern-poland.title: Kraków and southern Poland
krakow-and-southern-poland.lead: Wawel and the old town of Kraków, the salt mine of Wieliczka, Auschwitz, Częstochowa and two castles in Silesia.
krakow-and-southern-poland.intro: Kraków was the capital of the Polish kings, who were crowned and buried in the cathedral on Wawel hill, next to their castle. The route spends its first day there and then goes underground at Wieliczka, a salt mine worked for seven hundred years, with chapels carved out of the salt. It continues to the memorial and museum of Auschwitz-Birkenau, which asks for time and quiet, and to the monastery of Jasna Góra in Częstochowa, the most important place of pilgrimage in the country. It ends in Silesia with two very different castles: Moszna, all turrets, and Książ, on a rock above a wooded gorge.
stops: Basilica of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Kraków

austria-vienna-to-salzburg.title: Austria: Vienna to Salzburg
austria-vienna-to-salzburg.lead: Imperial Vienna, the Danube valley at Dürnstein and Melk, the lake of Hallstatt, the ice caves of Werfen and Salzburg.
austria-vienna-to-salzburg.intro: From the capital of the Habsburgs west to the city of the prince-archbishops. Vienna has the cathedral, the Hofburg, where the emperors lived, and the Belvedere of Prince Eugene. The route then follows the Danube through the Wachau, past the ruined castle of Dürnstein and the baroque abbey of Melk on its cliff. It turns south into the Salzkammergut for the lake of Hallstatt, below some of the oldest salt mines in the world, and reaches the Salzach valley at Werfen, with its castle and the largest ice cave on earth. It ends in Salzburg, under the fortress.
